standard.title: Managing emotions
standard.description: explain how and why emotional responses can vary and practise strategies to manage their emotions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have identified how different situations influence emotional responses (AC9HP2P03). They can identify emotional responses to situations but have not yet explained why responses vary or practised structured strategies for managing emotions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how and why emotional responses can vary and practise strategies to manage their emotions.

nodes.label: Triggers, warning signs and emotional responses
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify possible triggers and warning signs to predict emotional responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one trigger and one warning sign for a strong emotional response (e.g. frustration, anger, sadness) in a described scenario.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse multiple scenarios to identify triggers, warning signs and likely emotional responses; discuss how the same trigger can produce different responses in different people.
wider: Investigate how physical warning signs (heart racing, hands sweating, flushing) connect to emotional states, and explore how body awareness can help predict and manage emotional responses.
Explore how cultural backgrounds and family norms influence what triggers strong emotions and what is considered an appropriate response — using examples from different cultural contexts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising triggers and warning signs is the prerequisite for deliberate emotion management. Students who cannot identify the signals that precede a strong emotional response cannot apply self-regulation strategies at the moment they are needed — they can only reflect after the fact.

response_modes.reason: Students need a cause-effect scaffold for emotional analysis: trigger → warning sign → emotional response → consequence. Scenario analysis using a structured format (what happened, what did the person feel, what showed they were feeling that way, what did they do) builds this chain.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one trigger for a strong emotional response in a scenario.
Describes at least one warning sign that the emotion is building.
Explains the connection between the trigger and the emotional response.

nodes.label: Responding helpfully in emergencies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how someone might respond in a helpful way during an emergency.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least one helpful response a person could have in an emergency situation — including managing their own emotional reaction to help effectively.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a range of emergency scenarios and identify what helpful responses look like; discuss how managing one's own emotional state supports effective helping.
wider: Explore first aid or emergency response contexts where emotional regulation is critical for helpers — examining why staying calm is not just about the helper's comfort but about the quality of help provided.
Investigate how community members (e.g. emergency service workers, teachers) are trained to manage their emotional responses in order to respond helpfully.

response_modes.reason: Students need to see the functional connection between their own emotional state and their capacity to help others — this is not intuitive. A structured 'what happens to helping quality when the helper is panicking' analysis makes the link explicit.

success_criteria: Describes a helpful response someone could have in an emergency.
Explains how managing their own emotions would help them respond effectively.
Identifies one specific thing they could do to stay calm in an emergency.

nodes.label: Self-regulation strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can implement self-regulation strategies to manage the expression of emotional responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Practise at least one self-regulation strategy (e.g. deep breathing, counting, moving away) in a scenario or real context, and reflect on its effectiveness.
nodes.typical_width: Practise and compare a range of self-regulation strategies across different emotional scenarios; reflect on which strategies work best for them in different situations and explain why.
wider: Explore mindfulness-based self-regulation practices (e.g. guided breathing, body scan, visualisation) and practise at least one regularly over a period of time, tracking its effectiveness.
Investigate how athletes and performers use self-regulation strategies in high-pressure situations — applying one technique to a physical activity context.

response_modes.reason: Self-regulation in practice requires integrating trigger recognition (node 1) with deliberate strategy selection. Students who have practised both separately need opportunities to apply the full sequence — notice the trigger → apply the strategy — in scenario or real contexts.

No single self-regulation strategy works in all situations. Students benefit from practising multiple strategies (breathing, movement, self-talk, seeking support) and developing personal knowledge of what works for them.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: A diverse repertoire of self-regulation strategies — mindfulness, physical movement, cognitive reframing, help-seeking — is genuinely enriching and practically valuable. Wider students who develop and test multiple strategies build meaningfully more robust emotional management capability.
success_criteria: Practises at least one self-regulation strategy.
Identifies when in an emotional sequence the strategy should be applied.
Reflects on whether the strategy was effective and what they would do differently.
